This application is filed under Section 389(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking suspension of sentence.
2. The applicant herein is the accused in S.C. No. 746 of 2015 on the file of the Fast Track Special Court, Taliparamba, Kannur district.

entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
In the said case, he was charged for having committed offences punishable under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Sections 3(a)
r/w. 4, 5(l) r/w. 6, 5(m) r/w. 6 and 5(n) r/w. 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act).

entities.text: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act)
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: By the impugned judgment dated 18.04.2022, the applicant was found guilty under Section 376(2)(f) of the IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of Rs. 1 lakh with a default clause; to undergo imprisonment for life and to pay a fine of 50,000 for the offence under Section 5(l) r/w. 6 of the POCSO Act, with a default clause; to undergo RI for 10 years and a fine of 25,000, with a default clause for the offence under Section 376(2)(i) of the Indian Penal Code.
3. The short facts of the case is that the survivor was the niece of the appellant herein.
She was studying in the III Standard in the year 2012, whereas, the applicant was 21 years of age.
The mother of the survivor had expired and the minor child was living with her father and grandmother.

The prosecution allegation is that the appellant, on multiple occasions, misusing his proximity in family relationship with the child, subjected her to aggravated penetrative sexual abuse, during the period from 2012 to 2015.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that there is an inordinate delay in setting the law in motion.
The child has not given exact details of the time and date on which the sexual assault was allegedly committed by the appellant.
The prosecution witnesses have no explanation as to why despite the child disclosing the assault to her grandmother and father, they failed to report the incident to the police.

He would refer to the evidence of the survivor and it was submitted that the defence was able to bring out numerous discrepancies in her version which made it impossible to rely on the same to arrive at a finding of guilt against the appellant.
It is pointed out that though as per the prosecution, the appellant started abusing the child in the year 2012, she disclosed the fact to the PT teacher of the School only in the year 2015.

It is further submitted that the appellant, a man aged 21 years, has been serving his sentence since April 2022, and requests that, in view of the infirmities in the evidence adduced by the prosecution, it would only be just and proper to suspend the sentence and release the appellant on bail.
5. The learned Public Prosecutor has vehemently opposed the submissions.
She would urge that the appellant is a sexual predator, who, by misusing his close relationship with the child who was just 8 years in 2012, has subjected her to repeated penetrative sexual abuse.

She would refer to the evidence adduced by PW3, the Doctor, who examined the minor child and it was pointed out that the Doctor had noted that her hymen and fourchette were torn and there were bruises all over her vulva.
She would also refer to the evidence of the child and it is urged that the child has given evidence describing the despicable and horrible manner in which she was subjected to sexual abuse.

She would also refer to the evidence of PW2, the father of the child, who in cross-examination had stated in unmistakable terms that the fact of abuse of the child was brought to his notice and that in order to maintain his family's honor, he had failed to disclose the fact to the police.

Referring to the Xxxxx vs State Of Kerala on 8 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/114475798/
2 observations in Preetpal Singh v. State of U.P1., she submitted that unless the trial court's findings are palpably perverse, suspension of sentence in cases of grave sexual abuse involving minors is uncalled for.

sentences.text: She also emphasized that, at this stage of considering a suspension of sentence, the evidence is not to be re-evaluated in detail.

The principles that are to be borne in mind while considering an application for suspension of sentence after a finding of guilt has been arrived at by the trial court have been outlined by the Apex Court in Preet Pal Singh (supra), wherein it was held in paragraphs 35 and 38 as under:
35.

There is a difference between grant of bail under Section 439 CrPC in case of pre-trial arrest and suspension of sentence under Section 389 CrPC and grant of bail,
post conviction.

In the earlier case, there may be presumption of innocence, which is a fundamental postulate of criminal jurisprudence, and the courts may be liberal,
depending on the facts and circumstances of the case, on the principle that bail is the rule and jail is an exception, as held by this Court in Dataram Singh v. State of U.P.
[Dataram Singh v. State of U.P., [(2018) 3 SCC 22]

entities.text: Dataram Singh v. State of U.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Dataram Singh v. State of U.P., [(2018) 3 SCC 22]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, in case of post-conviction bail, by suspension of operation of the sentence, there is a finding of guilt and the question of presumption of innocence does not arise.
Nor is the principle of bail being the rule and jail an exception attracted, once there is conviction upon trial.
Rather, the court considering an application for suspension of sentence and grant of bail, is to consider the prima facie merits of the appeal, coupled with other factors.

There should be strong compelling reasons for grant of bail, notwithstanding an order of conviction,
by suspension of sentence, and this strong and compelling reason must be recorded in the order granting bail, as mandated in Section 389(1) CrPC.
xxxxxxx xxxxx   xxxx 38.

In considering an application for suspension of sentence, the appellate court is only to examine if there is such patent infirmity in the order of conviction that renders the order of conviction prima facie erroneous.

Where there is evidence that has been considered by the trial court, it is not open to a court considering application under Section 389 to reassess and/or re-analyse the same evidence and take a different view, to suspend the execution of the sentence and release the convict on bail.
7. Though the power to suspend an order of conviction, apart from the order of sentence, is not alien to Section 389(1) of the Code, its exercise should be limited to very exceptional cases.
Merely because the convicted person files an appeal in challenge of the conviction, the court should not suspend the operation of the order of conviction.
The court has a duty to look at all aspects including the ramifications of keeping such conviction in abeyance.
[See: K.C Sareen v. CBI, Chandigarh2].

While considering an application for suspension of sentence, the Appellate Court is only to examine if there is such patent infirmity in the order of conviction that renders the order of conviction prima Xxxxx vs State Of Kerala on 8 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/114475798/
3 facie erroneous.

Where there is evidence that has been considered by the trial court, it is not open to a court considering an application under Section 389 to reassess and/or re-analyze the same evidence and take a different view, to suspend the execution of the sentence and release the convict on bail.

8. Having considered the materials, we find that the innocent child who was a victim of brutal sexual abuse by the appellant disclosed to her PT teacher about the devious predatory acts of the appellant.

Evidence reveals that the child had intimated to her father about the sexual abuse to which she was subjected to, but the father, keeping the future of the child in mind, failed to report the matter to the police.
The Doctor who examined the child noted serious injuries on her intimate parts including a torn hymen and fourchette and injuries on her vulva.
The medical report clearly points to the fact that the child was subjected to penetrative sexual abuse.
The father while tendering evidence has (2001) 6 SCC 584 admitted that he had reprimanded and punished the accused when the fact of sexual abuse was brought to his notice.

The discrepancies pointed out by the learned counsel pale into insignificance when faced with the overwhelming evidence let in by the prosecution to prove the case of sexual abuse on a minor girl child under 10 years of age.

We find,
prima facie, that the learned Sessions Judge has evaluated the evidence in a proper and careful manner while arriving at the finding of guilt.
We find no patent infirmity in the order of conviction as forcefully contended by the learned counsel appearing for the appellant.
9. We are therefore of the considered opinion that the appellant has not made out any strong or compelling reasons for suspending the execution of the sentence.
This application is dismissed.
